extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, historians of mathematics, and mathematicians interested in foundations and mathematical practice (especially Bourbaki/structuralism)
extracted.subtask_description: Define what counts as a 'mathematical style' and analyze Nicolas Bourbaki as a case study of the structuralist mathematical style, extracting the constitutive patterns of definitions, inferences, presentation, and collaborative method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of a standard (contrast requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A style requires a 'standard', a way of doing mathematics against which the alternative style is contrasted; most of the time this standard is implicit and not recognized as such by the practitioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A purported style must be distinctive relative to an implicit or explicit community norm; identification of stylistic features depends on what is taken as the baseline practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of deviant patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: A style consists of a combination of patterns of behavior that deviate significantly from the standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single isolated variations do not amount to a style; there must be a coherent set of recurring choices (definitions, proofs, organization, computations) that together mark a departure from the community norm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic and voluntary use of patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: The patterns underlying a style must be used systematically and voluntarily; they must be implemented as a conscious value and applied broadly (not merely an occasional option).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners need not self-label their behavior as 'a style', but those behaviors must be repeated, recognizable, and (in the eyes of others) intentionally adopted rather than accidental. Styles tend to be taught and sustained across cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style as a global, systematic pattern of choices
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical style is a global and systematic pattern of choices made to define concepts, prove theorems, solve problems, compute formulas — i.e., a way of doing mathematics represented in presentations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasis on 'global' and 'systematic' distinguishes style from one-off methods or isolated heuristics; it includes language, notation, organization and recurring methodological priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical durability of style
rubrics_metrics.description: A style is intrinsically historical: it appears at some point and must last sufficiently long to be identified as such; it can later become the new standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identification requires temporal persistence; ephemeral or single-instance practices do not qualify. A style may lose 'style' status if it becomes the new, taught standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patterns of definitions (δ) differing from standards
rubrics_metrics.description: A corpus exhibits a style iff it rests upon specific and systematic patterns δ of definitions that differ significantly from the standards of the cultural context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patterns of definition include choice of language (symbolic, diagrammatic), introduction of new languages, and systematic ways of defining classical objects (e.g., set-theoretic Cartesian product vs categorical universal-property product).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patterns of inference (ι) differing from standards
rubrics_metrics.description: A style requires specific and systematic patterns ι of inference that differ significantly from community standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patterns of inference are shaped by the language/definitions chosen; they can include reliance on computational inferential 'black boxes', diagrammatic reasoning, or other characteristic proof techniques (e.g., coupling algebraic computation with geometric inferences). Examples: Cartesian/Leibniz vs Weierstrass styles; homotopy type theory proofs that follow new inferential paths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinations κ of definitions and inferences differing
rubrics_metrics.description: A style includes combinations κ of components of δ and ι in problem-solving and organization of concepts that deviate significantly from standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This captures how particular definitional choices and inference patterns are combined to solve problems; the combined effect (not just individual parts) constitutes the style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transportability / invariance under isomorphism (structuralist principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Structuralist styles require that properties and relations used to define structures be 'transportable' (invariant under the appropriate notion of isomorphism): if P(X) and X ≅ Y then P(Y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a key structuralist criterion of identity and legitimacy of definitions; it motivates doing mathematics 'up to isomorphism' and selecting frameworks where such transportability is formalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria of identity for abstract structures (isomorphism/equivalence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patterns of definition must include explicit criteria of identity for abstract structures (e.g., isomorphism; in later developments homotopy/categorical equivalence or higher equivalences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A structuralist style emphasizes identity conditions appropriate to the structures at hand; failure to specify identity (or choosing a different criterion) marks a different style (Weil vs Bourbaki example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate logical/metamathematical framework
rubrics_metrics.description: A style requires an appropriate logical framework to codify its inference patterns (e.g., first-order logic/set theory for set-based structures; FOLDS or homotopy type theory for more modern needs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of logical framework affects what counts as valid patterns of inference and what structures can be handled (e.g., categories, higher equivalences). The framework must support the structuralist principle and 'transportability'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic framework to combine and compare structures (category/functor emphasis)
rubrics_metrics.description: A structuralist style requires a systematic apparatus to combine and compare abstract structures (categories, functors, operations that relate species of structures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bourbaki originally relied on axiomatic/set-based means; later developments show categories/functors provide a more effective systematic language. The presence or absence of such a framework is a stylistic marker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do mathematics 'up to isomorphism' / maximality principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Characteristic of Bourbaki: identify the appropriate abstract structures, work with them in their most general form (maximality), and solve problems by applying theorems about these structures — i.e., mathematics is done up to isomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contrasts with a minimality approach (start with the simplest specific context). The maximality approach often requires deep knowledge of many abstract structures and may be seen as more abstract or elitist but provides powerful general results and unifying explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatic, abstract exposition (method of exposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposition proceeds axiomatically and abstractly, normally from the general to the particular; aims to provide a solid foundation and relies on a rigorously fixed logical order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manifested in prefaces ('To the Reader') and in text structure: everything is built from axioms/definitions/theorems; the utility of some considerations may not be immediately apparent to the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global logical organization (book/chapter dependency rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Global rule: each statement assumes as known only those results discussed in preceding volumes/chapters; precise indication of logical relationships is given to avoid vicious circles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This enforces a strict dependency graph across material; it is a hallmark of Bourbaki's edifice-like organization and aids formal clarity and avoidance of hidden assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local logical framework (definitions, axioms, theorems as core recallable parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Within a chapter the logical framework consists of definitions, axioms, and theorems — these are the parts to bear in mind for subsequent use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presentation emphasizes a tight theorem-proof (Satz-Beweis) sequence; local structure supports reuse and transportability of notions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation style: terse, austere, and minimal (no informal motivations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presentation is extremely dry, severe, austere, unified and terse: few images, no informal motivations or narrative, and few extraneous examples or commentary; results are presented efficiently with necessary components only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This stylistic choice values elegance, economy, and logical cleanliness; anti-patterns include discursive rambling, informal heuristic motivation, or surplus examples that break the logical compactness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative, iterative editorial method (unanimity and ruthless criticism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Production method: collaborative drafting with repeated congresses where chapters are read aloud and criticized point-by-point; multiple successive drafts (often many) and a rule of unanimity (single veto can block publication) lead to final texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This brutal, iterative process shapes the presentation and content (definitions weighed, proofs criticized, organization analyzed). It is a production-style criterion: who/how produces the text matters for the resulting style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expository orientation of volumes
rubrics_metrics.description: Bourbaki's Éléments are primarily expository treatises (not research monographs), designed to systematize existing mathematics in an abstract, axiomatic presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The expository aim explains choices like breadth, ordering, and emphasis on foundations rather than on novel proofs or research narratives; style expectations differ between expository and research genres.
